articles.title: Database report shows which entities take up space
articles.dek: A Storage report identifies the tables and entities taking up space, including on Core and Container installations.
body: A new Database card breaks down Home Assistant’s history storage by table and entity. Administrators can search and sort the entity list to find what takes up space, then open an entity’s settings from the report.

The report separates recorded states from statistics, making it easier to find a particularly busy sensor or a large collection of retained history. Per-entity sizes are estimates; some database configurations can report row counts without byte sizes.
A Refresh button measures the database when requested. The card also brings the Storage page to Core and Container installations that use the recorder.

articles.title: Shutter and blind drawings become controls
articles.dek: A redesigned panel keeps the reported position separate from the position requested.
body: Tap or drag a shutter, blind or garage-door drawing to choose its position in Home Assistant’s redesigned cover panel. Labeled Open, Stop and Close buttons sit alongside it.

The picture follows the position reported by the device, while a separate marker shows the requested position. That keeps a command from looking like a movement that has already happened. Covers without position control use an open-or-close gesture instead.
The control also supports keyboard and screen-reader operation. Where a cover supports tilt, a switch changes between position and tilt controls.

articles.title: Z-Wave JS UI puts the network on a floorplan
articles.dek: Routes, battery levels and network health appear alongside the rooms where devices sit.
body: An uploaded floorplan puts Z-Wave devices in their physical context, with network connections drawn between them. In Z-Wave JS UI, owners can maintain separate maps for different floors or buildings and drag devices into position.
Optional layers show current and backup routes, failed connections, neighbor links and battery levels. Clicking a device opens its usual details, and maps are included in backups by default.

Steve Berg tested the view on a network of about thirty-seven devices. Owners place devices on the map themselves, and route information builds as devices communicate, so a map can initially lack routes after a restart.

articles.title: Android brings camera talkback to local HTTP connections
articles.dek: The companion app supplies the microphone connection when the browser cannot.
body: Talking through a compatible camera gains a microphone path on local HTTP connections in the Home Assistant Android app. A native connection supplies the audio when the browser cannot.
The app requests microphone permission before starting and stops the stream when the page closes or the app moves into the background. The camera still needs to support two-way audio.

articles.title: A simpler Marketplace starts with what people want to do
articles.dek: A proposal groups community projects by type and goal, and explains what to do after installation.
body: Finding a community project by the problem it solves is the aim of a new Home Assistant Marketplace proposal. Laura (@laupalombi) is shaping one Discover page with routes by type—such as dashboard cards, integrations and themes—and by goals such as tracking energy or adding devices.

A proposed detail page puts a plain-language summary and the next step after installation above the developer’s README. It would explain where a card or theme appears, keep updates visible on the Installed page, and identify the project as community-made and not tested or reviewed by Home Assistant.

The plan uses existing catalog information apart from a small curated set of goal-based lists. Who maintains those lists, how they fit with integration categories, and the mobile and dark-mode designs remain open questions. The installation process itself is outside this proposal.

articles.title: A new sign-in route restores ARD Sounds accounts
articles.dek: Device-code sign-in restores subscriptions and listening progress without storing an ARD password.
body: ARD Sounds listeners get a replacement for the password login that stopped working in Music Assistant: a device code confirmed on ARD’s own sign-in page. The change restores account access after ARD restricted password login to its captcha-protected website and moved subscription data out of the API the provider used.

Subscribed podcasts synchronize with the Music Assistant library, and listening progress travels in both directions, with the newer position taking precedence. Adding or removing an ARD podcast also changes the subscription in the ARD account.

Existing password-based accounts need to sign in again. Radio, search and public podcasts continue without an account, while an account-service outage preserves the existing subscription list. Peter Meiser tested sign-in, subscriptions, listening progress and session renewal with a real account.

pullRequests.title: Fix ARD Sounds account login and sync subscriptions and progress

articles.title: Long chapter lists become easier to follow
articles.dek: Segmented timelines and chapter titles carry across the player, queue and detail pages.
body: Audiobook and podcast chapters get their own timeline segments in Music Assistant’s web player, with “Chapter X of Y” between the timestamps. The fullscreen player leads with the current chapter’s title, while the book or episode and its author remain underneath.

The queue lists chapters and bookmarks with their start times and keeps the current chapter in view. Detail pages separate those entries into tabs and highlight the chapter playing. Tapping the chapter count switches between chapter progress and progress through the whole book or episode.

The change applies to AI-assisted broadcasts; VoIP phones remain outside them.

articles.title: Zonneplan exposes its price schedule to automations
articles.dek: A new action returns hourly or quarter-hourly rates for planning around cheaper electricity.
body: Planning around cheaper electricity gets a fuller set of rates through a new Zonneplan action in Home Assistant. It returns each interval’s start, end and all-in price per kilowatt-hour from the data already fetched for the account, for both hourly and quarter-hourly contracts.

That gives an automation the full available schedule to compare, rather than just the current or next price and daily extremes—for example when finding a cheaper block for charging. Calling the action does not make another request to Zonneplan.

articles.title: Reolink recordings get a picture before you open them
articles.dek: Recording previews help identify footage, while thumbnail loading leaves room for playback.
body: A frame from each Reolink recording replaces its blank placeholder in Home Assistant’s media browser. Cards that use the same media source can use those previews too.

The media browser also limits simultaneous local thumbnail requests and cancels ones that are no longer needed. That keeps a page of previews from occupying every connection while someone tries to play a recording. Michał Jonik makes a first contribution to Home Assistant Core with the recording previews.

body: Crossfade and Autoplay become switches for each Music Assistant player’s queue in Home Assistant. They can be placed on a dashboard or used in an automation, alongside the integration’s playback controls.
The entities require Music Assistant 2.11 or later; older servers do not receive them. Fabian Munkes contributes the integration change and documentation.

articles.title: A manual address reaches DLNA players discovery misses
articles.dek: An advanced setting accepts a device address or its description URL.
body: Speakers and receivers missed by automatic discovery gain a manual-device setting in Music Assistant. Owners can enter an IPv4 address or an HTTP or HTTPS device-description URL, giving DLNA equipment on a routed network another route into the player list.

A device address triggers a targeted discovery request; a description URL connects directly. Offline manual devices are retried every minute. Mark (@m-a-r-k-e) tested the URL route with a Denon receiver on a separate network segment, making a first contribution to Music Assistant’s server. The receiver did not answer targeted discovery, so the address route remains device-dependent.

body: Asking what a thermostat is set to becomes distinct from asking for the measured temperature in Dutch Assist. Temperature questions also work for a whole floor, including floor names used directly, such as “beneden”.
Martijn van der Pol adds phrases for setting covers by name in a room or on a floor, and for setting a class of covers on a floor. Related additions switch off lights or fans across a floor.

articles.title: ESP32 light configurations move away from NeoPixelBus
articles.dek: ESPHome changes a deprecation warning into a configuration error and points makers to the RMT LED-strip platform.
body: Existing ESP32 light configurations using NeoPixelBus need to switch to esp32_rmt_led_strip before they can pass validation with the updated ESPHome software. The former warning becomes a configuration error.
The platform had already warned that support would end when ESPHome moved to ESP-IDF 6. This change does not remove NeoPixelBus support from ESP8266 devices.

articles.title: Backup Wi-Fi works when a preferred hidden network is absent
articles.dek: An ESP32 fix stops failed hidden-network probes from blocking the next configured connection.
body: An ESP32 device can move on to its next saved Wi-Fi network when the preferred hidden network is out of range, following a correction in ESPHome. Previously, a delayed notification from the failed attempt could trap the device in repeated retries.

The correction covers both ESP32 frameworks. On an ESP32-PICO-D4 bench setup, it connected after all four resets, while the affected build failed to connect during the comparison runs. ESP8266 devices were not affected.

pullRequests.title: [wifi] Join the next network after a failed hidden network probe on ESP32

articles.title: Z-Wave restores protect controller identity and update keys
articles.dek: A restore safeguard covers older controller firmware, with a limit when the backup ends in data.
body: Controller identity and firmware-update keys get protection from a backup-restore hazard in Z-Wave JS. Restoring a backup could erase a neighboring part of the controller’s memory; on Home Assistant Connect ZWA-2, losing that manufacturing information changes its security identity and prevents signed firmware updates.

The driver avoids writing through the hazardous boundary when a backup ends in unused space, extending protection to older firmware. If its final byte contains data, the restore still proceeds with a warning. The author has verified the safeguard with unit tests, but has not tested it on hardware.

pullRequests.title: fix: work around NVM restore erasing the flash page after the NVM

articles.title: Readings recover after a device restart
articles.dek: Shutdown ordering prevents a stale state from hiding an unchanged reading when the device reconnects.
body: A restart or firmware update could leave an ESPHome entity marked unavailable in Home Assistant even after the device reconnected. A shutdown correction prevents queued readings sent after the disconnect notice from making the next identical reading look like a duplicate.

Devices without deep sleep send the queued readings their connection can accept before announcing the disconnect. Deep-sleep devices keep their existing order so an expected sleep remains distinguishable from a lost connection.
